title: Choking adult: clearing a blocked airway
asks: someone is choking what do I do
how to do the heimlich maneuver
he is choking and cant talk
back blows or abdominal thrusts for choking
choking person passed out now what
choking pregnant woman what to do
airway obstructed by food pt conscious
food stuck in throat turning blue
answer: Ask if they can speak or if they are choking. If they can speak or cough effectively, encourage them to keep coughing and do not interfere.
If they cannot breathe, speak or cough, or make only high-pitched sounds when breathing or coughing: call for help and act immediately.
Give back blows and abdominal thrusts, and keep going until the object is expelled or the person becomes unresponsive.
Back blows: have the person bend at the waist and strike the back between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand, in the direction of the head, five times.

Abdominal thrusts: stand behind the person and wrap your arms around their waist. Make a fist with one hand and grasp it with the other, thumb side against the abdomen, in the midline slightly above the navel but well below the tip of the breastbone. Press into the abdomen with a quick backward and upward thrust. Make each thrust a separate and distinct movement.

Advanced pregnancy, a markedly obese person, or a significant abdominal wound: use chest thrusts instead. Stand behind with your arms under their armpits, place the thumb side of your fist on the middle of the breastbone, grasp it with the other hand and thrust.
If the person becomes unresponsive: call for help, lay them face up on a firm surface and open the airway. Sweep an object out of the mouth only if you can see it.

Then attempt rescue breathing. If the air will not go in, give chest thrusts: kneel close beside the person, heel of the hand on the lower part of the breastbone, the other hand on top, elbows locked, and press down and release quickly and distinctly.
Repeat chest thrusts, checking the mouth and rescue breathing as long as necessary to clear the object. If the chest rises, feel for a pulse.
warnings: A blocked airway starves the brain of oxygen and leads to unconsciousness and, if not promptly corrected, death. Quick action is essential.
Do a finger sweep only if there is a visible obstruction in the mouth, to avoid pushing the obstruction deeper.

quotes.text: To assess and manage airway obstruction, start by asking the casualty if they can speak or if they are choking. Additionally, check for the universal choking sign (see figure 5-11 on page 67). If the casualty can speak or cough effectively, encourage them to continue coughing. This indicates that they still have good air exchange, and you should not interfere with their efforts to expel the obstruction.

However, if you notice high-pitched sounds when the casualty breathes or coughs, indicating poor air exchange, or if the casualty is unable to breathe, immediate action is required. Call for help and prepare to perform manual thrusts to clear the obstruction. Use abdominal thrusts, also known as the Heimlich maneuver, by positioning your hands between the waist and the rib cage and delivering quick upward thrusts. For individuals in advanced stages of pregnancy, those who are markedly obese, or if there is a significant abdominal wound, use chest thrust instead. This involves placing your hands in the center of the breastbone and pushing sharply inward and upward.

Encourage the person to speak or cough if possible and observe if the obstruction is removed. Do not perform the manoeuvres described below if the person is audibly coughing and/or able to make sounds. A person who is unable to speak or cough has complete airway obstruction and needs immediate help:
have the person bend at the waist and give five back blows (with the heel of your hand, strike the back between the shoulder blades in the direction towards the head).

Abdominal thrust can be accomplished by using the following procedures: • Stand behind the casualty and wrap your arms around their waist. • Make a fist with one hand and grasp it with the other. The thumb side of your fist should be against the casualty's abdomen, in the midline and slightly above the casualty's navel, but well below the tip of the breastbone (figure 5-12 on page 68). • Press the fists into the abdomen with a quick backward and upward thrust (figure 5-13 on page 68).

Each thrust should be a separate and distinct movement. • Continue performing abdominal thrusts until the obstruction is expelled or the casualty becomes unresponsive. • If the casualty becomes unresponsive, call for help as you proceed with the steps to open the airway.

Stand behind the casualty and wrap your arms around their chest with your arms under their armpits. • Make a fist with one hand and place the thumb side of the fist in the middle of the breastbone (take care to avoid the tip of the breastbone and the margins of the ribs). • Grasp the fist with the other hand and exert thrusts (figure 5-14 on page 69).

If a conscious individual begins choking and subsequently loses consciousness, immediate action is required: • Summon help right away to ensure assistance is on the way. • Open the casualty's airway to assess and manage the obstruction. • Perform a finger sweep only if there is visible obstruction in the mouth to avoid pushing the obstruction deeper. • Attempt to rescue breathing, which involves assessing whether the air can flow into the lungs.
If the choking person becomes unconscious, lie him/her face up on a firm surface. Performing chest thrusts may relieve the obstruction.
To perform chest thrusts the unresponsive casualty is placed on their back, face up, and open their mouth. The first responder kneels close to the side of the casualty's body and—

Place the heel of the other hand on the lower half of the breastbone next to the two fingers (figure 5-16 step B on page 71). • Remove the fingers from the notch and place that hand on top of the positioned hand on the breastbone, extending or interlocking the fingers (figure 5-16 step C on page 71). • Straighten and lock elbows with their shoulders directly above the hands without bending the elbows, rocking, or allowing the shoulders to sag. • Apply enough pressure to depress the breastbone 1½ to 2 inches and then release the pressure completely (figure 5-16 step D on page 71). This press and release process is delivered quickly and distinctly, six to 10 times.

The first responder repeats the sequence of the chest thrust, finger sweep, and rescue breathing as long as necessary to clear the object from the obstructed airway. If the casualty's chest rises, proceed to feeling for their pulse.
However, it's critical to recognize that an obstructed airway can lead to oxygen deficiency in the brain, resulting in respiratory arrest, unconsciousness and, if not promptly corrected, death.

Quick action is essential in these situations to restore breathing and prevent further complications, including death. Always ensure to assess the situation carefully and apply the appropriate technique based on the casualty's condition

conflict: ORDER OF BACK BLOWS AND ABDOMINAL THRUSTS (the card gives no order): ATP 4-02.11 (2026) para 5-33 says give five back blows before abdominal thrusts, then continue abdominal thrusts until the obstruction is expelled or the casualty becomes unresponsive; WHO-ICRC Basic Emergency Care 2018 says give five abdominal thrusts first, then, if the obstruction persists, five back blows, and repeat thrusts followed by back blows. UNRESPONSIVE CASUALTY (the card gives chest thrusts, which both allow): ATP 4-02.11 paras 5-36 to 5-41 say attempt rescue breathing, then 6 to 10 abdominal thrusts (kneeling astride the thighs) or chest thrusts (breastbone pressed 1½ to 2 inches, six to 10 times), repeating thrusts, finger sweep and rescue breathing; WHO BEC says chest thrusts, then rescue breaths and chest compressions per CPR protocols. Number of thrusts for a conscious person: WHO says five at a time; ATP gives no number. HHS Ship's Medicine Chest 2003 (crew first-aid assessment standards, older guidelines) differs again: for a conscious adult, abdominal or chest thrusts only (no back blows) until effective or the victim becomes unconscious; for an unconscious adult, one standard says up to 5 abdominal or chest thrusts, then tongue-jaw lift and finger sweep, and another says CPR with no abdominal thrusts or mouth sweeps. ATP 3-50.21 (2018) says during CPR look in the mouth for an object before breaths and remove it if seen. FEMA P-2064 (2020) has nothing on choking.

review.notes: Problems, per check (c): (1) No usable sequence. A3 says 'Give back blows and abdominal thrusts, and keep going', A4 gives 5 back blows, A5 gives abdominal thrusts with no number, and nothing says to alternate. The sources each give a full cycle but disagree on the order: ATP 4-02.11 5-33 'Prior to applying abdominal thrust, first responders should administer five back blows', then thrusts until expelled; WHO BEC 'Pull in and up five times... If the obstruction persists... give five back blows... Repeat abdominal thrusts followed by back blows'. Fix: state the cycle on the card with both orders attributed (5 back blows then abdominal thrusts, ATP; 5 abdominal thrusts then 5 back blows, repeated, WHO) and say to keep cycling until it comes out or they collapse. (2) Unresponsive: the card stops at 'If the chest rises, feel for a pulse' with no next step. WHO BEC: 'If a series of chest thrusts is not successful, continue with rescue breaths and chest compressions based on relevant CPR protocols.' Fix: add 'If there is no pulse, start CPR, checking the mouth for the object before each set of breaths.' Confirmed: ATP 5-30 to 5-41 (assessment, cough = do not interfere, abdominal and chest thrust technique, pregnancy/obesity/abdominal wound, finger sweep only if visible, unresponsive sequence), WHO (do not intervene while coughing). No PDF junk. Minor: ATP gives 6-10 chest thrusts per set for the unresponsive person; the card gives no number.
